name: Bagobo-Klata
confidence_why: Estrera 2022, the only first-hand phonology available, shows seven penult/ultima minimal pairs and calls stress contrastive, and because Bagobo-Klata has no phonemic vowel length his remark that stress is "predictable from vowel length" describes the long-vowel correlate of penultimate stress rather than a competing weight rule, so the lexical reading rests on one solid source with the earlier accounts (Cagas 1991, Evans 2017) unobtained.

catalog_quote: In this study, segmental stress is defined as the prominence (i.e., loudness) of a specific syllable in a given word (Crystal 2008). First, in Bagobo-Klata, segmental stress is contrastive, as shown in Table 11. [Table 11: Contrastive stress in Bagobo-Klata — Penultima / Ultima: [ˈɁuː.la] ‘snake’ / [Ɂu.ˈla] ‘rain’; [ˈpɔː.tɔj] to ‘quarrel’ / [pɔ.ˈtɔj] ‘to kill’; [ˈbaː.sa] to ‘read’ / [ba.ˈsa] ‘squash’; [ˈɁɔː.lat] ‘scar’ / [Ɂɔ.ˈlat] ‘vein’; [ˈkuː.luŋ] to ‘snore’ / [ku.ˈluŋ] ‘back’; [ˈɁaː.tiŋ] ‘sweat’ / [Ɂa.ˈtiŋ] ‘if’; [ˈlaː.wu] ‘cloud’ / [la.ˈwu] to ‘fall’] Second, stress is also predictable because of vowel length. Table 12 shows that stress falls on the ultima (i.e., light (CV) or heavy (CVC)) if there is no vowel length. ... On the other hand, Table 13 shows that if a word has vowel length, stress falls on the penultima. ... [Conclusion, p. 266] Synchronically, Bagobo-Klata has 20 phonemic speech sounds—15 consonants and five vowels. Besides speech sounds, geminates, consonant clusters, and segmental stress are shown to be contrastive.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on one of the last two syllables and is lexically contrastive between penult and ultima (minimal pairs like [ˈɁuː.la] 'snake' vs [Ɂu.ˈla] 'rain'). A stressed open penult always carries a long vowel, so the author equivalently states it as: final stress (CV or CVC ultima) when the word has no long vowel, penultimate stress when the penult vowel is long. Vowel length is not set up as an independent phoneme, and the conclusion lists stress (not length) among the contrastive features, hence coded lexical; a weight-sensitive (long-penult-else-final) reading is the same facts under the length-primary analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphophonology (sec. 7.1, p. 253): the irrealis PV -ɔ, B/LV -a and nominalizing -a delete the antepenult of the affixed form 'while the stress shifts to the penultima' (e.g. ha.ˈwɛt + -ɔ -> ha.ˈwɛː.tɔ -> ˈwɛː.tɔ). CVC ultimas do not attract stress differently from CV (both final-stressed absent length). Antepenultimate stress not attested in the data shown (trisyllables/quadrisyllables in Table 8 are penult- or final-stressed).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on citation forms from a 1,026-item elicited wordlist (roots mostly mono/disyllabic); phonetic transcriptions mark primary stress and penult vowel length throughout the paper. No phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Bagobo-Klata (endonym Klata; exonym Giangan/Jangan/Guiangan), ISO bgi = Glottolog gian1241, spoken on the eastern slopes of Mt. Apo, Baguio/Calinan/Tugbok districts of Davao City; Estrera and Zorc 2019 both state Giangan and Klata are the same speech community. Data from a 1,026-word list; no dialect differentiation made. Note Glottolog's booktitle for Estrera 2022 ('Studies in the Anthropology of Language in MSEA') is wrong: the paper is in 'Papers from the 30th Conference of SEALS (2021)', JSEALS Special Publication 8, pp. 244-284 (Wikipedia's 283-323 is also wrong).

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record has an empty rule; the existing statement (drawn from this same paper) labels it 'lexical (unpredictable)' from the Table 11 minimal pairs. The full section adds that stress is 'also predictable because of vowel length' (no length -> ultima; long penult -> penultima), plus the affixation-triggered shift to the penult. Compatible with the contrastive penult/ultima statement but the better label is weight-sensitive (length-conditioned) or, if length is taken as underlying, lexical penult-vs-final; 'unpredictable' overstates what the source says.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Disyllabic words carry stress on either the penult or the final syllable, and minimal pairs exist (Table 11). The placement is predictable from vowel length: if the penult vowel is long, stress is on the penult; if there is no long vowel, stress is on the final syllable, whether it is CV or CVC (closed final syllables do not attract stress on their own, e.g. [lɔm.ˈmɔɁ] 'morning', [ta.ˈlum] 'papaya'). Length and stress co-vary, so the system can equally be labelled as a lexical penult-vs-final contrast carried by vowel length (Philippine type); Estrera himself calls it both 'contrastive' and 'predictable because of vowel length'.
new_statements.exceptions: Under affixation with -ɔ/-a (irrealis PV/BLV, nominalizer) the antepenult is deleted and 'the stress shifts to the penultima' (sec. 7.1, p. 253, ex. 15-17: ha.ˈwɛt + -ɔ -> ha.ˈwɛː.tɔ -> ˈwɛː.tɔ); syncope deletes the unstressed penult nucleus of words like /bɔl.ˈlɔj/ when affixed (sec. 7.7). Sec. 1.1 (p. 244) notes that Cagas (1991) and Evans (2017) also treat segmental stress but faults Evans for unsupported generalizations; no other paper in the volume mentions Klata.
new_statements.identity_note: Estrera 2022 describes Bagobo-Klata (endonym Klata, exonym Giangan) as spoken on the eastern slopes of Mt. Apo, Davao City (Baguio, Calinan and Tugbok districts) and Barangay Don Panaca, Magpet, Cotabato (p. 244); no separate dialect is named, so the statement applies to the language as a whole.

readall_conflicts: Only one source was listed and it was already held by the project; no disagreement between sources. The one internal tension is in labelling: Estrera 2022 says segmental stress is contrastive (minimal pairs, sec. 6 Table 11; Conclusion p. 258) and in the next sentence that it is predictable from vowel length (long penult vowel -> penult stress, otherwise final). The existing statement recorded 'lexical (unpredictable)'; the source supports 'weight-sensitive / length-conditioned penult-vs-final' at least as well, and the catalog's empty rule field should be filled with the penult-if-long-else-final rule. Cagas (1991) and Evans (2017), which Estrera cites as also treating stress, were not obtainable (no open copy).

sources.note: Section 6 'Segmental Stress' (pp. 252-253): stress is contrastive (7 minimal pairs penult vs. ultima, Table 11, penult-stressed member always with a long penult vowel); 'also predictable because of vowel length': ultima (CV or CVC) if no vowel length (Table 12), penultima if the word has vowel length (Table 13). Sec. 7.1: affixes -ɔ/-a delete the antepenult and stress shifts to the penult. Conclusion (p. 266) lists segmental stress among the contrastive features. Vowel length is not listed as a phoneme.

tone.quote: Stress is shown in Klata by an increase in loudness/intensity and pitch, rather than duration. Lexical stress is predictable. There are some exceptions, but they number less than 10 per word type from a dataset of several thousand. … • Stress and prosody is a huge area we’ve barely touched upon.
tone.locator: Sec. 5.2 Default Stress, p. 75; second part ch. 8 Questions for Further Research, p. 86
tone.summary: No statement on lexical tone; pitch named only as a cue of word stress (with loudness). Stress predictable: trochaic feet built right to left, primary stress on the penult; prosody called unstudied.
